Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pesd-.

From late Middle High German huchen, of unclear origin. Diebold argues that it must be an early or pre-Proto-Indo-European substrate borrowing (anywhere from the eastern Pontic to the western Kirghiz steppes) and compares other fish of uncertain origin like salmon and char.

parole.significato: to mumble, to murmur, to mutter (a word, sentence, etc.)
parole.testo: From a Proto-Indo-European *mur- (“to murmur”), which appears to be onomatopoeic; see Latin murmur (“murmur”) for more cognates. Note also murren (“to grumble”).

parole.significato: to thrust down, to knock down (to hit or knock (something) so that it falls)
parole.testo: From nieder (“down”) + stoßen (“thrust”), from Old High German stōzan, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd-.

parole.significato: to work in a careless, sloppy manner; to slack; to botch
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German slampen, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lembʰ- (“to hang loosely”), for which see Schlamm (“mud”) for more. See also Schlampe.

parole.significato: to purr (produce a vibrating, whirring sound, especially when satisfied)
parole.testo: From Middle High German snurren, ablaut variant of snarren (whence modern schnarren), ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend); compare Dutch snorren, as well as English snarl. Uncertain; compare Middle High German senen (“sadness, grief, heartache”). Has been considered a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-, though whether in the "sow (seed)" or "longlasting" sense is unclear.

From Middle High German spræjen, spræwen, ultimately from some derivative of Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to sprinkle, scatter, strew”), see also Latin spargō, English sprout. Compare Middle Dutch sprayen, spraeyen, Dutch sproeien (“to spray”). See spray for more.

parole.significato: tight, firm, of an object that could also be slack
parole.testo: From late Middle High German straf, cognate with Dutch straf, with further origin uncertain. However, a semantic connection Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter(h₁)- (“to be stiff; be rigid; exert”) (whence Proto-Germanic *staraz (“stiff”)) has been proposed (DWDS).
From Middle High German strūchen, from Old High German strūhhōn, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streug-, *streuk-, extended from *ster- (“stiff”).
Perhaps cognate with Old Norse stolpi (“post”) (compare Norwegian Bokmål stolpe) and Latvian stulbs. Ultimately maybe from Proto-Indo-European *stel-.

From Middle High German traz, from an unknown source whence also Dutch tarten (“to provoke, dare”). From Middle High German wanst, from Old High German wanast, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-. Cognate with Latin venter (“belly”) and Latin vēsīca (“bladder”).
